Their subject is RNA-seq, a lab method that counts how active each gene is in a sample. Comparing those counts across samples sounds simple, but small sample sizes and wild swings in the numbers mislead older methods.

DESeq2 steadies the estimates by sharing strength across genes. It shrinks the noisiest fold changes toward safer values and handles samples with very few repeats. The authors call this moderated estimation. Labs studying cancer, infection, and basic cell life now run DESeq2 by default, and the paper is one of the most cited in its field.
plos-pone-0000049:
Akiko Kashiwagi, Itaru Urabe, Kunihiko Kaneko, and co-authors offered a theory of how gene networks adapt, in a 2006 paper. A gene network is a web of genes switching each other on and off. When the environment changes, the network must settle into a new pattern of activity that keeps the cell alive.

Their proposal is fitness-induced attractor selection: the network wanders among stable states, called attractors, and the state that raises fitness is the one that sticks. Adaptation, on this view, is partly the network trying states and keeping what works. The theory gives evolution inside a single cell a mechanism, and it has influenced how theorists model flexible genomes.
cia-0000139449: Project SUN STREAK, the United States government's remote viewing effort of the 1980s, is the program behind document 0000139449, dated 1988. Under the program, trained viewers tried to describe distant places and events by mental means alone, and staff wrote up the sessions. This record is one such file from the program's later years. The whole strange venture was declassified in the 1990s, and its papers remain a unique corner of Cold War intelligence history.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d49: Secretary of State Cordell Hull wrote to President Roosevelt on October 21, 1943, from the Moscow Conference. His letter is Document 49 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Hull had traveled to Moscow for the first three-power meeting of foreign ministers, a trip few had expected the aging secretary to make. The record names the parties and the date. What Hull reported home must be read in the printed text.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d149: Roosevelt wrote to King Farouk of Egypt on November 20, 1943, on the eve of the Cairo Conference in the king's capital. The letter is Document 149 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. A courteous letter to a host king was standard summit manners, and Egypt's young king ruled the land where the leaders were about to meet. The record names the two men and the date. The text is printed in the volume.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d249:
The calls paid on President Roosevelt at Cairo on the afternoon of 22 November 1943 are covered by an editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume. No records of these conversations have been found, and the editors draw their account from the President's Log and from Admiral Leahy's diary.

Leahy records tea at Kirk Villa with the President, Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek, Madame Chiang, General Marshall, and Harry Hopkins. Churchill's visit, the note says, presumably took place apart from the Chiangs' call. Nothing in the surviving evidence suggests that weighty problems were discussed at either visit, and the editors judge both to have been courtesy calls.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d349:
Elmer Davis, director of the Office of War Information, sent Brendan Bracken, the British minister of information, a secret priority protest from Washington on 30 November 1943. Its subject is a Reuters dispatch from Lisbon that had given away the Cairo Conference a day before the official announcement.

Davis concedes that Reuters is a private firm beyond British government control, yet the dispatch was passed by British censorship for radio abroad while kept out of British papers. He lists the harms. First came a perilous breach of security. Then lost political value, since Germany and Japan could blanket the world with their own version first. Last came the fury of American reporters who had kept extraordinary secrecy. He calls the leak the worst of many such incidents and warns it could become a grave obstacle to Anglo-American understanding.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d449:
From December 5, 1943 comes this further agreed record of a United States-United Kingdom meeting at the Second Cairo Conference. Both delegations approved the wording, which makes agreed minutes one of the firmest kinds of evidence in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume. The conference was then in its final stretch.

Readers find the joint account of what the two governments put on record that day, while the military chiefs met in parallel and the Tehran pledges awaited detailed plans. Set beside the British and American minutes of the same date, this text lets a reader test one side's memory against the other's. That cross-checking is how sound summit history gets built.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d549:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull wrote to President Roosevelt on January 19, 1944, in the continuing exchange between the department and the traveling summit's home base. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

By mid-January the questions flowing between Hull and Roosevelt included the follow-up to Tehran's pledges and the building of a postwar organization, Hull's great project. The Secretary's health and influence were both waning that year, but his channel to the President remained busy. For readers, the message shows routine at the top of wartime government: regular, formal, and carrying real decisions inside its courtesies.
frus-1944-quebec-d49:
Roosevelt replied to War Shipping Administrator Emory Land on September 2, 1944. The reply came the day after Land's message. The exchange appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

A presidential answer within a day shows urgent shipping business. Such business could not wait in a queue. Land's agency fed every theater and ally. Its allocations shaped what the Quebec Conference could promise. For readers, the pair brings a binding subject into view. Hulls and cargo space rarely draw attention. Without them, no strategy agreed in Canada could move. Not one division would have sailed.
frus-1944-quebec-d149:
General Wilson expanded his theater review for the War Department on September 8, 1944, in telegram Naf 774. The Dragoon transfer to Eisenhower was in hand, so the message concentrates on Italy and the Balkans. In Italy, Alexander's offensive had been running since August 26, and Wilson weighed two futures for Kesselring's army.

If the Fifth Army's coming offensive hammered the Germans before they could withdraw in order, Wilson foresaw decisive results and pursuit toward the Ljubljana Gap and Brenner Pass. If demolitions and bad weather covered an orderly retreat, only the Lombardy Plain could be cleared that year. In the Balkans he expected German forces trapped south of the Danube, and a small force stood ready to occupy Athens.
frus-1944-quebec-d249: An editors' note records a preparation that went unused. frus-1945-malta-yalta-d49: Roosevelt wrote back to Churchill on 9 January 1945, answering the prime minister on the day his letter came. Document 49 in the Foreign Relations volume on Malta and Yalta preserves the reply, as published by the Office of the Historian. The rapid back-and-forth of that week shows two governments synchronizing their positions before meeting Stalin together in the Crimea.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d149:
British newspapers were blaming Washington for Mikolajczyk's fall, and Stettinius moved to correct them. His memorandum to the President of 28 November 1944 is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It encloses two telegrams, one on the premier's reasons for resigning and one quoting the London press.

A number of British papers, he reports, wrongly lay the resignation to an American refusal to guarantee Poland's frontiers. To counter the stories, the Department issued a statement on 25 November. A frontier guarantee, it said, was not and could not have been an issue. The government's long-standing policy of never guaranteeing set frontiers in Europe was well known, and it stood.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d249:
Roosevelt told Churchill on 4 October 1944 that the Soviet staff would see the allied plan for Japan. These excerpts of his telegram number 626 are printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The editors' note spells out what the plan asked of Russia.

American military men in Moscow, the President writes, will make the Joint Chiefs' statement to Stalin available to the prime minister. That statement set the missions for Soviet forces in a joint war. They were to secure the Trans-Siberian Railroad and the Vladivostok peninsula. Allied air forces would strike Japan from the Maritime Provinces and Kamchatka. Sea lanes between Japan and the mainland would be cut, Japanese forces in Manchuria destroyed, and the port of Petropavlovsk opened for American naval use.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d349:
Radios and newspapers carried this agreed text on February 7, 1945: the Crimean Conference's first word to the world. The release states that the three leaders, with their chiefs of staff and foreign secretaries, are meeting in the Black Sea area. Their aim is to finish the defeat of the common enemy and to build firm foundations for a lasting peace.

Meetings, it says, are going on without pause. The conference opened with military talks, a full review of every European front, and a complete exchange of information. Complete agreement for joint operations in the final phase is claimed. The text tells the public much, while naming neither Yalta nor a single decision.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d449:

London welcomed word that Soviet authorities had agreed to stop removing equipment from fields where British interests were involved. The Ruat plant, too, would remain in place. If the removed equipment was not returned, London argued, it must count as deliveries on account of reparations. Compensation for the oil companies should be arranged. frus-1945-potsdam-1-d49:
Stalin confirmed the meeting date once more in a personal and secret message to President Truman on June 3, 1945. It is document 49 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference, printed from the Truman Papers. Stalin had received Truman's message of June 1 and replied from Moscow two days later.

The message is only two sentences long. Stalin notes Truman's cable and repeats that he has already written that he agrees to July 15 as an entirely suitable date for the meeting of the three. With Germany defeated, that date set the timetable for the Potsdam Conference, where the Allies would take up the shape of postwar Europe.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d149:
President Truman replied to Ambassador Patrick Hurley in China in a top secret telegram dated June 4, 1945. The message is document 149 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Hurley had sent frank reports on the military situation in China and on what he saw as the worldwide aims of America's European allies.

Truman thanks him for the candor and says the matters are getting full consideration in American planning. He has no official word that Britain wants command of the Chinese armies, he adds, and sees no gain in changing the present command setup in China. Many of Hurley's questions, he notes, may be taken up at the coming three-power conference. A note lists the questions: Hong Kong's future, trusteeship for Indochina, and support for democratic government in China.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d249:
Ambassador Tarchiani pleaded Italy's colonial case in a memorandum to President Truman dated July 6, 1945. The extract printed here is document 249 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The memorandum sets out the position, wishes, and hopes of the new Italian government.

Italy has willingly abandoned the Fascist dream of empire in East Africa, Tarchiani writes, though she spent more than 36 billion lire building modern systems there. Libya, he argues, is national territory, administered like Italy's home provinces. Eritrea and Somaliland are Italy's oldest colonies, where Italian capital and labor brought civilization, and their people, he claims, favor continued Italian rule. He asks that Italy's rights be recognized in some form that spares her modest African holdings and her national dignity in a moment of distress.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d349:
What the United States meant to achieve in Germany troubled a Central Secretariat paper of July 12, 1945. Marked SC-145, it suggests the Staff Committee send the Secretary a statement of views for the Berlin meeting. The aim was a clearer definition of the government's objective in occupying Germany. A draft by MacLeish is attached.

The draft states the problem bluntly. Signs suggested that no common agreement existed on the American purpose in the occupation. No full definition of purpose could be found in existing papers, and the directives for each phase of the occupation did not rest on one. frus-1945-potsdam-1-d449:
London's qualifications on Greek elections fill a British Embassy paper of July 10, 1945, paraphrasing a Foreign Office telegram of July 9. The proposal that invitations to the Soviet and French governments be issued by the Americans and British, not by the Greek government, is not strictly in line with the Varkiza Agreement. It might cause some resentment in Athens.

Nevertheless, the Foreign Office does not regard these objections as too serious. It is prepared to support President Truman's proposal, particularly as time is getting short. But it is strongly opposed to advising the Greek government to hold elections before the plebiscite. That, London argues, is Greek internal politics, to be settled by Greeks.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d549:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff sent President Truman a top secret memo on July 7, 1945. Signed by General George Marshall, it is document 549 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The subject was the sharp shortage of troop ships for the Pacific war.

The chiefs say General MacArthur's needs have grown, and deficits will last through late 1945. Seven captured passenger ships in European ports could carry 37,500 troops in all. The largest is the Europa, rated at 10,000 men. The chiefs urge Truman to ask the prime minister for all seven ships for U.S. troops. A draft letter to Churchill is attached, and the question of who ends up owning the ships is put off.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d649:
Lowell Pinkerton, the consul general at Jerusalem, sent a secret assessment of Palestine on July 10, 1945. It is document 649 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Washington had asked what might follow an adverse British ruling on Jewish immigration.

Pinkerton cites the inspector general of police, who does not expect a general Jewish uprising. Large-scale illegal immigration, though, is predicted, and preparations in the Balkans are already reported. Terror attacks by the Stern group and the Irgun are expected against the British. Many in both the Jewish and Arab communities, he adds, are armed and some are well trained. The largest body, the Hagana, is well disciplined. It would act as a group only on its leaders' orders, if Arabs attacked after terrorist provocation.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-49:

Byrnes proposed that the council meet not later than September 1. Molotov asked what day of the week that would be, and Eden answered that it was a Sunday. Molotov said he agreed, and the date was settled in those terms. The talk then turned to the council's composition. Molotov asked if five members were meant, noting that composition would decide what questions the council could take up. Byrnes answered that the first meeting, in London, would be of five. frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-149:

frus-1945-potsdam-2-d849:

frus-1945-potsdam-2-d949:

frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1049:

He urges that Britain be pressed hard to change course, and to keep shipping usable coal to Europe at the old rates.

America's own six million ton allocation for Europe will draw fire at home, he warns. Domestic heating shortages loom, and shipping and rail capacity are strained. If British exports stop at the same moment, the outcry will grow. Guyon gives simple steps for beginners: read a little, then pause and be still before God. She warns against forced feelings and showy methods. quicherat-proces-jeanne-darc-vol5-1849:

heart-sutra-muller-sbe49:
A few hundred words hold the core of Mahayana Buddhism in the Heart Sutra. The Heart Sutra, in the English rendering of Friedrich Max Müller from 1894, gives that core text in full. Müller's version stood in the Sacred Books of the East, the great Victorian shelf of world faiths.

The sutra says form is emptiness and emptiness is form, and sweeps away each prop the mind would clutch. Monks and lay folk chant it daily from Tibet to Japan. Its end is a mantra that promises passage to the far shore of waking. No Buddhist text so short carries so much weight.
lot-no-249:

project-sign-report-1949:
Project Sign was the United States Air Force's first true study of flying saucers. Its tech report of February 1949 sums up the first year of work. Air Materiel Command ran the study from Wright Field. The report was kept from the press at the time and freed much later.

Case by case, the staff weigh pilot tales, photos, and bits of proof. Some tales get plain causes, while a few stay unexplained in their lists. Staff talk hints that some men leaned to a bold view of the craft. The report is the root file of the state's saucer work.
hahnemann-organon-1849:
Samuel Hahnemann was a German doctor who broke with the harsh cures of his day. His Organon of Medicine lays out the scheme he called homeopathy. Charles Dudgeon's English dress of 1849 brought the work to British readers. The book is the root text of the whole school.

Like cures like, Hahnemann holds: a drug that makes a sign in health can cure that sign in the sick. He bids the doctor use the least dose that can still act. Rules for case work and drug tests fill the text. Homeopaths still treat the book as law.
law-spirit-of-prayer-1749:
William Law wrote The Spirit of Prayer in 1749, late in his life. Law was the English priest whose Serious Call had moved a whole age. Here he turns to prayer as the core of all true faith. The book had force with mystics and with the Oxford men of a later age.

Law holds that prayer is not a set of words but the soul at work. The wish for God, he says, is prayer in its true form. He warns off cold rites and bids the heart burn with plain want. The short book is a deep draught of English soul lore.
poe-von-kempelen-and-his-discovery-1849:
Edgar Allan Poe put out Von Kempelen and His Discovery in 1849. The tale is a brief hoax in the dress of news. A man named Von Kempelen is held by the law in New York. In his rooms the law finds a craft that turns lead to gold.

Gold falls in price in the tale's world as word of the find spreads. Poe plays the whole thing dead straight, with dates and trade facts. He had just scored with a hoax on a chess craft years past. The tale is a sly probe of crowds, news, and greed.
bronte-shirley-1849:
Charlotte Brontë published Shirley in 1849, her ambitious condition-of-England novel of the mills. The tale is set in Yorkshire against the Luddite risings of 1811 to 1812. It was the first major industrial novel by a woman in English letters of the time.

Mill owner Robert Moore brings new machines as starving weavers plot to smash them at night. Shirley Keeldar, a brisk heiress, and meek Caroline Helstone view his world from two sides. Caroline pines in a parsonage while Shirley runs her estate and teases her old tutor. A shooting, a mad dog's bite, and two weddings close the social panorama of Yorkshire. Brontë wrote it in grief, as her brother and sisters died around her.
dumas-queens-necklace-1849:
Alexandre Dumas published The Queen's Necklace in 1849, second of his Marie Antoinette romances in French. The romance retells the Diamond Necklace Affair, the scandal that helped doom Marie Antoinette in France. Its mix of court splendor and fraud was drawn from trial records and memoirs of the time.

Jeanne de la Motte forges the queen's name to steal a necklace meant for Madame du Barry. Cardinal de Rohan, duped by a fake queen in a midnight grove, signs for the gems. Cagliostro, the occult count, moves through salons as police close in on the fraud at Paris. The trial cleared the queen in law but ruined her in the public mind of France. Dumas makes the affair a tragedy of pride, hunger, and a court's decay.
thoreau-civil-disobedience-1849:
Henry David Thoreau published Civil Disobedience in 1849, first as Resistance to Civil Government in print. The essay states the duty to resist unjust government and charters nonviolent civil disobedience for later ages. Thoreau wrote it after a night in jail for refusing a poll tax in protest.

He protested slavery and the Mexican War, which he saw as a slave power land grab. The essay holds that conscience outranks statute, and a just man must break an unjust law openly. Under a government which imprisons any unjustly, he wrote, the true place for a just man is prison. Gandhi and King both drew on its logic in their campaigns of nonviolent mass action later. Its brevity and moral force make it Thoreau's most influential single piece of prose.
thoreau-week-on-the-concord-1849:
Henry David Thoreau published A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers in 1849, his first book. The river journey with his brother John fills its seven days of rowing, camping, and talk. The elegy contains the seed of Walden in its praise of wildness, friendship, and simple days outdoors.

Thoreau printed the book at his own risk, and most copies came back unsold to his attic. John had died of lockjaw in 1842, and the voyage of 1839 became a memorial in prose. Each day mixes natural notes with essays on books, friendship, history, and the soul's quiet hours on rivers. Hindu scriptures and English poets float beside fish, locks, and New Hampshire hills in its wide-ranging pages here. Unsold in its day, it is now read as the overture to Walden's fame.
parkman-oregon-trail-1849:
Francis Parkman published The Oregon Trail in 1849, an account of his own journey west in 1846. Parkman, a young Bostonian in poor health, rode from St. Louis along the emigrant trail. He hunted buffalo, met wagon trains, and lived for weeks with a band of Oglala Sioux. Forts, prairies, and mountain passes mark the route.

Parkman writes what he saw with energy and sharp detail. His judgments reflect his age and class, and modern readers note his bias toward Native peoples. Even so, the book became the classic American frontier narrative. It gives the West as lived experience, not legend. Later western writing starts here.
castro-de-iusta-haereticorum-punitione-1:

Three books weigh what heresy is, which penalties the law allows, and how rulers and judges should act. Castro argued for firm punishment but also set limits and urged care in proof. He drew on scripture, church law, and past cases to build his rules. The work is a key source for how learned churchmen defended persecution in law, and why they thought mercy toward heresy was a public danger.
pascal-provincial-letters-pearce-1849:

Letter by letter, Pascal pretends to learn from Jesuit teachers how their moral rules work. Their own words, calmly repeated, expose lax excuses for sin and easy pardons for the rich. The comedy is dry, the logic tight, and the damage lasting. The letters fixed Pascal's fame as a prose master. They also helped make satire a serious art in French writing.
storm-immensee-1849:

School, travel, and slow years apart let another man win Elisabeth's hand. A late visit to her home shows both what was lost and what duty built instead. project-grudge-report-1949:

herodian-history-hart-1749:

Eight books hold Commodus on the throne, the year of five emperors, the Severan house, and the chaos of the third century. Herodian writes as a minor official who saw courts at close range. His tale is vivid, moral, and often sharp. For these years he is one of the few full sources that survive.
haddock-somnolism-psycheism-1849:

zoist-vol-07-1849:

smith-dictionary-greek-roman-biography-m:

fielding-tom-jones-1749:

plos-pone-0004149:

plos-pone-0004249:

geneva-convention-1-1949:
The first of the four Geneva Conventions of 1949 protects wounded and sick soldiers in armies on land. Nations redrafted the rules in Geneva after the Second World War, building on a line of agreements going back to 1864. The aim was to make sure that a soldier out of the fight through wounds or sickness is never treated as fair game.

The articles require armies to collect and care for the wounded of both sides, without favor. Medical staff, ambulances, and hospitals are protected, and the red cross emblem marks that protection. Attacking the wounded or those who care for them is forbidden. Nearly every nation on earth has accepted the 1949 conventions.

The second Geneva Convention of 1949 carries the protection of the wounded to warfare at sea. It adapts the older Hague rules and the land convention to sailors, marines, and others fighting on the water. Two world wars had shown how exposed the wounded and shipwrecked were when ships went down far from help.

Under its articles, the wounded, sick, and shipwrecked at sea must be rescued and cared for by whichever side finds them. Hospital ships are protected from attack and capture, and their crews must be respected. The convention also covers coastal rescue craft and medical aircraft over the sea. Together with its three sister conventions, it forms the core of modern war law.
geneva-convention-3-1949:
Prisoners of war are the subject of the third Geneva Convention of 1949. Written after a war in which prisoners had been starved and murdered in great numbers, it sets firm limits on captors. The text builds on earlier prisoner rules from 1929 that had too often been ignored.

Captured fighters must be treated with respect, given enough food and shelter, and shielded from insults and public display. They may send and receive mail, and the Red Cross may visit their camps. Torture and medical experiments are banned outright. When the fighting ends, prisoners must be sent home without delay, a standard still cited in every modern conflict.
geneva-convention-4-1949:
Civilians in wartime gained their own full shield in the fourth Geneva Convention of 1949. Earlier war law had guarded soldiers and prisoners, while civilians in occupied lands were left with thin protection. The deportations and mass killings of the Second World War made the gap impossible to ignore.

The articles ban murder, torture, hostage-taking, and collective punishment against civilians under an army's control. Forced deportation from occupied land is forbidden, and children, the sick, and the wounded get special care. Occupying powers must keep food and medical supplies flowing to the people under their rule. The convention remains the main legal guard for civilians caught in modern wars.

The signers were the United States, Canada, and ten European states still rebuilding from the Second World War. Fear of Soviet power in Europe drove them to bind their defense together in peacetime.

The heart of the treaty is Article 5, which treats an armed attack on one member as an attack on all. Members promise to help the victim, including with armed force if needed. Volume 1 lays out the theory that all thought grows from linked sensations. Simple impressions join into complex ideas, feelings, and habits through repeated pairing. The scheme made the mind look like a machine of habit, which thrilled some readers and alarmed others. James Mill and later psychologists built on Hartley's foundation, and the book stands as the founding work of association psychology.

On 16 July 1945 the acting secretary of state wrote to Norman Armour, the American ambassador in Spain. The message left Washington on the day before the Potsdam Conference opened. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Spain stood apart from the war's endgame, ruled by Franco and watched with suspicion by the victors. An ambassador there needed clear guidance on how far to go with a regime the Allies disliked but had to handle. This instruction shows the department tending a hard post at a busy hour, and it widens the volume's map beyond the summit grounds in Germany.
frus-1945-50-intel-d49:
Another paper prepared for the Secretary of State's Staff Committee is dated 26 November 1945. It follows the committee's 168th meeting by six days. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Committees consume papers the way furnaces consume coal, and a second staff paper in a week shows the intelligence question still burning at State. Drafters wrote these papers knowing the secretary's senior men would test every line. Readers can compare this paper with the one prepared on 15 November to see the department's thinking move. That movement, visible across the November run, is the sound of a bureaucracy closing in on its final ask.
frus-1945-50-intel-d149:
Dated 7 May 1946, this memorandum runs from the Director of Central Intelligence (Souers) to the President’s Chief of Staff. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 149, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. Washington was still building a peace-time spy service, run for the moment by the National Intelligence Authority and the Central Intelligence Group.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d249:
A text titled "Report by an Ad Hoc Subcommittee of the State–Army–Navy–Air Force Coordinating Committee" bears the date 7 November 1947. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 249 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The CIA was only weeks old, having replaced the Central Intelligence Group in September 1947 under the National Security Act.

Findings come first in a reader's eye, but the body of a report is where the proof sits, fact by fact. The replies it drew, kept near it in the files, show how the findings stood up to attack. Subcommittee reports did the detailed work for the full committee, weighing facts and drafting the choices the main body would vote on.
frus-1945-50-intel-d349:
A memorandum dated 1 July 1948 was prepared for a named reader. The reader was the President of the Discussion at the 14th Meeting of the National Security Council. It is document 349 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The Cold War was turning harder that year, and the new Council and CIA were being tested by it week by week.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1861-d49:
Writing to London on 3 June 1861, William H. Seward directed Charles Francis Adams on the summer's work. The letter is document 49 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

June orders from Seward pressed Adams to watch British shipyards and ports. Southern agents were already seeking ships and arms in Britain. The letter shows the contest moving to docks and yards, where quiet work by consuls and envoys could stop a warship before it sailed. Southern agents in London worked through ship brokers, which made the yards a front of the war. Quiet work in the yards saved more Union ships than any note could.
frus-1861-d149:
From Paris on 29 August 1861, William Dayton closed the month with a report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 149 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Dayton closed August with word from a Paris grown used to the war. The crisis mood had cooled into a watchful calm. His letter shows the French file settling into the long routine that would mark the rest of the year. A watchful calm in Paris was worth an army corps to the Union that autumn. Good value in a calm report is a theme the autumn file repeats with cause.
frus-1861-d249:
A dispatch dated 28 August 1861 carried word from James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands to William H. Seward in Washington. Congress received it as Document 249 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. The letter comes from the first summer of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d49:
A State Department letter of 16 April 1862 told Charles Francis Adams what Washington wanted done. Congress received it as Document 49 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. By then, in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d149:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, sent word to Charles Francis Adams in London on 23 September 1862. Adams held the post of American minister to Britain. Their exchange is printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume, where this letter appears as Document 149.

The day before, Lincoln had made public his plan to free enslaved people in the rebel states. British leaders now had to weigh a war that was openly about slavery as well as union. Regular dispatches let Seward steer his envoy's talks in London while British opinion took shape in the proclamation's first days. No working cable crossed the Atlantic in 1862, so every answer waited on a mail steamer.
frus-1862-d249:
Dated 23 January 1862, Document 249 is a dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris. It is printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume, in the section given to France.

Late January found the allied move on Mexico under way and the American war entering its second calendar year. Seward kept Dayton on a short, steady leash of written orders, since a cable across the Atlantic did not yet exist. Letters like this one carried both policy and tone: firm on the war, careful not to provoke Paris. Dayton's French was limited, and he leaned on his staff and on careful written notes.
frus-1862-d349:
On 11 December 1861 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Henri Mercier, the French minister in Washington, in a letter printed as Document 349 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The catalog title gives the name as Merrier.

Seward wrote in the heart of the Trent crisis, when his handling of foreign envoys was being tested daily. France's minister mattered because Paris often moved in step with London on American questions. A letter to Mercier in that week was both business and signal: Washington meant to deal fairly with France while the British storm blew. Mercier had served in Washington since 1860 and knew the capital's politics at close range.
frus-1862-d449:
On 6 August 1861 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Baron Friedrich von Gerolt, Prussia's minister in Washington. The note is Document 449 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the annual message.

Seward wrote a fortnight after the Union defeat at Bull Run, when foreign ministers were recalculating the war's likely length. Gerolt, Prussia's veteran envoy, was a channel to one of Europe's friendlier courts. Notes of this kind kept resident ministers supplied with the government's view and handled the steady business between the two states. The letter is part of the 1861 foundation of the Prussian file, laid down while the war's shape was still unclear to everyone.
frus-1862-d549:
On 30 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this note to Roest van Limburg. It is Document 549 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Seward closed September with the Dutch file in good order, answering the minister's late-month notes in his prompt fashion. The emancipation order was now a week old, and its effects were beginning to reach the legations. Between the United States and the Netherlands the practical questions stayed what they had been: ships, trade, and the rules of neutrality. The note is a routine piece made interesting by its moment. Its writer knew the routine itself was a form of reassurance. Friendly powers took comfort from it.
frus-1862-d649:
On 24 May 1862, Robert H. Pruyn wrote from his post in Japan to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 649 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. Pruyn had lately succeeded Townsend Harris, the first American minister sent to Japan.

Letters from the Japan legation dealt with trade, the safety of Americans there, and the mood of the shogun's court. Pruyn's report is one of those working papers, not a speech or a treaty. It earns its place because the full run of such letters is the best record we have. It shows how the two lands dealt with each other in the 1860s.
frus-1863p1-d49:
Stephen R. Mallory wrote this letter to James M. Mason on 26 October 1862. Mallory was the Confederate secretary of the navy; Mason was the South's envoy in London. The letter is document 49 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The navy office's stake in London was ships. Southern buyers in Britain were having warships built in its yards, and Mason stood watch over that work. Mallory's letter belongs to that file, the sea side of the South's push abroad. Printed in the Union's record, it pairs with the Adams letters in the same volume, where the other side fought to stop those very ships.
frus-1863p1-d149:
The legation sent three letters on 9 April 1863; this one, from Charles Francis Adams to Secretary of State William H. Seward, opens the set. Three Adams letters in the volume bear the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 149 in part one of the 1863 volume.

A three-letter day in mid-April shows the post still at full stretch after the raider's seizure. Adams covered the yards, the law, and the talk of the town in his split sheets. This one opens the set of 9 April. The run of his April mail is a close record of the ship fight's turn, kept by the man who fought it from the legation.
frus-1863p1-d249:
An instruction dated 24 July 1863 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, in London. It appears as document 249 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Confederate agents were buying ships and arms in Britain, and Washington wanted the trade stopped. Orders to London often carried protests, evidence, and legal arguments for Adams to use. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d349:
To Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this formal note on 3 January 1863. It appears as document 349 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Canada, then a British colony, shared a long border with the Union. Worries about raids, plots, and smuggling across that line sit behind part of this correspondence. It dates from the month the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, which changed the politics of the war in Britain at once. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d449:
A letter of 6 April 1863, from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, stands as document 449 in the printed record. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d549:
The date 5 June 1863 heads a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d649:
The 26 October 1863 mail between Washington and London included a letter from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. Mail between London and Washington crossed the Atlantic by steamer, so each reply took weeks to complete the round trip. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them.
plos-pbio-0020049:
Christopher V. Rao, John R. Kirby, and Adam P. Arkin compared how two bacteria steer toward food in PLOS Biology in 2004. E. coli and Bacillus subtilis both swim toward good chemicals and away from bad ones, a behavior called chemotaxis. They use related genes but wire them in different ways.

The study asks what stays the same when the same job is built twice. Core sensing steps match, yet the control loops differ in telling ways. That mix of sameness and variety is a gift for engineers of living systems. It shows which parts of a circuit are fixed by the task and which parts evolution felt free to change.
plos-pone-0000149:
Marian Warsame, Omari Kimbute, Zena Machinda, and colleagues published this malaria study from rural Tanzania in PLOS ONE in 2007. It examines how families and health workers recognize severe malaria, what they think causes it, and how they treat it. A focus is rectal artesunate, a drug given as a suppository before a sick child can reach a hospital.

Severe malaria kills fast, so what happens before referral often decides the outcome. The authors record local beliefs and treatment habits that a pre-referral drug program must work with. The findings guide how new treatments get introduced in villages, where custom and distance can matter as much as the drug itself.
plos-pone-0000249:
Susanne Prinz, Christine Aldridge, Stephen A. Ramsey, and colleagues published this systems biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. In yeast, the MAP-kinase pathway is a chain of signals that helps the cell respond to stress. The authors show that an RNA-binding protein controls signaling in that pathway, adding a layer of regulation beyond the kinases themselves.

RNA-binding proteins adjust which messages get used, and here one tunes a whole signal chain. The finding connects two control systems that were often studied apart. It matters for the basic wiring diagram of the cell, in an organism used to model processes in many others.
plos-pone-0000349:
Tini Garske, Paul Clarke, and Azra C. Ghani published this poultry flu study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It estimates the transmissibility of highly pathogenic avian influenza in commercial poultry in industrialised countries, how fast the virus spreads within and between industrial farms. The authors draw on outbreak data from such settings.

Transmissibility numbers decide culling and control policy when an outbreak hits a poultry-dense region. Industrial farms, with huge flocks in sheds, behave differently from backyard flocks. The paper supplies estimates fitted to that reality, for planners preparing for H5N1 and its relatives.
plos-pone-0000449:
Lusisizwe Kwezi and colleagues tested a plant hormone receptor for a hidden talent, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The receptor is AtBRI1 of Arabidopsis thaliana, which senses brassinosteroids, steroid hormones that steer plant growth. The team found that part of the receptor functions as a guanylyl cyclase in vitro, an enzyme that makes the signaling molecule cyclic GMP.

A receptor with its own enzyme activity can pass a signal in two ways at once. Showing the activity in the test tube is the first step; the bigger question is whether the plant uses it. The study adds a candidate pathway to how steroid signals move through plant cells.
plos-pone-0000549:
Matthew E. Hardee and colleagues blocked a blood-vessel growth signal and watched tumors stall, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Erythropoietin is known for making red blood cells, but it also helps trigger tumor angiogenesis, the growth of new vessels that feed a tumor. The team showed that erythropoietin blockade inhibits the induction of angiogenesis and tumor progression.

The finding cuts two ways. It flags a risk: anemia drugs that mimic erythropoietin might feed tumors. And it suggests an opportunity: blocking the signal could starve them. Work of this kind reshaped how oncologists thought about a routine supportive drug during the years that followed.
plos-pone-0000649:
Michaela Lucas, Axel Ulsenheimer, Katja Pfafferot and colleagues followed helper T cells through acute hepatitis C infection, in PLOS ONE in 2007. CD4+ T cells provide help that keeps antiviral immune responses going. In infections that resolve, that help is sustained. In infections turning chronic, helper responses appear absent or short-lived.

The team tracked virus-specific CD4+ T cells during the acute phase and after it. Watching the same response over time shows where chronic cases lose their support. The contrast matters for vaccine thinking, since a vaccine must raise help that lasts. It also helps explain why some hepatitis C infections clear and others settle in.
plos-pone-0000749:
Gregory P. Henderson, Lu Gan and Grant J. Jensen pictured the inside of one of the smallest eukaryotic cells in 3D, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Eukaryotic cells divide their functions among membrane-bound organelles. Modeling that ultrastructure accurately has been hard: light microscopy lacks resolution, and older electron methods introduce artifacts. Their subject, O. tauri, is a tiny marine alga.

Using electron cryotomography, they imaged an entire cell frozen in place, slicing the data into a three-dimensional model. A whole-cell map at molecular detail shows how organelles pack into minimal space. O. tauri's small size makes it a natural lower limit for eukaryotic design.
plos-pone-0000849:
Mamadou B. Coulibaly, Neil F. Lobo, Meagan C. Fitzpatrick and co-authors traced how a flipped stretch of DNA in the malaria mosquito may have been born. Anopheles gambiae, Africa's main malaria carrier, holds many such flips, called inversions. They help it thrive in many settings across tropical Africa. A first step to grasp how flips arise is to read the DNA at their break points in fine detail.

The team's title points to segmental duplication as the likely cause of one flip, named 2Rj. A copied stretch at a break point can make chromosomes misalign, and the piece between them can flip. How flips form sets how fast mosquitoes can lock helpful gene sets together.
plos-pone-0000949:
Mark Read, Gordon Grigg, Steve Irwin and colleagues tracked moved crocodiles by satellite, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Estuarine crocodiles are secretive, spread over remote country and easily disturbed. How far they can travel was poorly known, a gap that matters when problem animals are relocated.

The team fitted transmitters to translocated adults and followed their movements after release. The title tells the headline: the crocodiles made long coastal journeys and homed back. Moving a large predator may not solve a local conflict if it simply returns. Tracking data like this should shape how wildlife agencies handle crocodile removals.
plos-pone-0001049:
Olaf Sporns, Christopher Honey and Rolf Kotter mapped the hub regions of brain networks, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The cortex is wired by bundles of fibers linking region to region. Earlier analyses counted connections, motifs and path lengths in those networks.

The authors set out to identify and classify hubs, the heavily connected regions that hold a network together. Hubs carry the traffic between specialized areas. Damage to a hub should matter more than damage elsewhere, a prediction with clinical weight. Their classification gives brain mapping a shared vocabulary for the regions that sit at the center of the web.
plos-pone-0001149:
Most gene-expression studies of cancer focus on one tumor type at a time. Yan Lu and co-authors took a broader approach in a 2007 PLOS ONE article, searching for cancer genes shared across tumor types. They used integrated analysis of gene-expression data, the microarray measurements of which genes are active in a tumor.

Combining data sets across cancers offers more patients for validation than single studies usually have. The authors report common human cancer genes found by this integrated route. Genes that recur across many cancers are attractive targets, since a drug aimed at one of them might help in several diseases.
plos-pone-0001249:
The Anopheles gambiae species complex is a set of closely related mosquitoes, only some of which transmit malaria well. Rui Wang-Sattler and colleagues used fingerprint genotyping of 414 field-collected female mosquitoes to reconstruct the group's history, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Three decades of attempts had gone into that reconstruction, since it guides malaria control strategy.

The authors describe a mosaic genome architecture in the complex: different genome regions tell different evolutionary stories, because genes have crossed between forms. A mosaic history complicates the idea of fixed species boundaries. It also affects how resistance and other traits spread among these mosquitoes.
plos-pone-0001349:
How the descendants of a fertilized egg first commit to becoming nerve tissue is an old debate. Is neural induction merely the default path, or does it need instructive cues? Nibedita Lenka and Saravana Kumar Ramasamy used embryonic stem cells to address the issue, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their monoculture strategy avoided cell-cell interaction effects that complicate other systems.

The authors conclude that neural induction from ES cells portrays default commitment but instructive maturation. In other words, cells drift toward a neural fate on their own, but need signals to mature properly. Their answer splits the debate rather than settling it for one side.
plos-pone-0001449:
Timothy Lesnick and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study that extends a gene path test from Parkinson's disease to a second ill. The second ill, called ALS, kills the nerve cells that move muscles. The team had built models from variants in axon guidance genes. Those models had strongly flagged Parkinson's risk and course.

They asked whether the same path also flags ALS risk. A shared path would hint that both ills grow from like faults in nerve wiring care. Gene path tests look at sets of genes at once, not one by one. That wider lens can catch weak signals that single gene hunts miss.
plos-pone-0001549:
Fiona Lees, Mark Baillie, and George Gettinby published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on sea lice drugs in Scottish salmon farms. Sea lice are a pest that plagues farmed salmon and wild fish near farms. Farms lean on a few drugs to curb them, which risks the lice growing resistant. The team reviewed one key drug's record from 2002 to 2006.

They weighed how well the drug still worked across farms and years. A slow slide in effect would warn of resistance on the rise. Such reviews guide when to switch or rest a drug. They also serve wild fish health, since lice spill from farms to wild stocks.
plos-pone-0001649:
Mia Phillipson, Jaswinder Kaur, Pina Colarusso, and their co-authors filmed white blood cells leaving blood vessels in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Neutrophils, the most common white cells, exit the blood at sites of inflammation to fight infection. Swelling builds up at the same spots. Cells can leave between vessel wall cells or straight through them.

The team describes dome-like covers that vessel wall cells raise over neutrophils as they cross. These endothelial domes seem to seal the crossing point, limiting how much fluid leaks out and how much the vessel wall opens up. The full text gives the imaging and leak measurements. Sealing each crossing helps explain how tissues can call in defense cells without flooding themselves.
plos-pone-0001749:
Paola Finocchietto, Fernando Barreyro, Silvia Holod, and their co-authors studied insulin's control of muscle mitochondria in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Mitochondria are the cell's energy plants. In metabolic syndrome, with excess insulin in the blood, suppressed mitochondria may help muscle store fat and glycogen and speed the syndrome's progress. Nitric oxide had emerged as a reversible brake on mitochondria.

The team reports that insulin's control of muscle mitochondria entails activation of an Akt2 and mitochondrial nitric oxide synthase pathway. The full text gives the pathway tests and energy measures. Linking insulin to a mitochondrial brake helps explain how high insulin can paradoxically slow energy burning in muscle.
plos-pone-0001849:
Adele Murrell, Yoko Ito, Gaetano Verde, and their co-authors studied methylation changes at a growth-control locus in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Differentially methylated regions are associated with many imprinted genes, genes whose activity depends on which parent they came from. In mice, methylation at a region upstream of the H19 gene is acquired in the male germline. That region, the imprint control region IC1, influences methylation 100 kilobases away.

The team reports distinct methylation changes at the IGF2-H19 locus in congenital growth disorders and cancer. The full text gives the patient samples and methylation maps. This locus is the classic imprinting example; its faults cause both overgrowth and growth restriction syndromes.
plos-pone-0001949:
Colette Smit and co-authors modeled why HIV patients fare differently across Dutch clinics, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Once drug therapy starts, survival in the first three years varied by treatment center. One suspect was timing: how late people enter care after infection sets the stage for all that follows.

The team built a math simulation fed with data from the ATHENA cohort, a national record of HIV patients. As the title states, late entry to care limits what therapy can achieve. The model shows how much of the gap between clinics is set before the first dose is ever given.
plos-pone-0002049:
Irina Buhimschi and co-authors mined the fluid around unborn babies for signs of early birth, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Preterm birth has many routes, and new protein tools had lately shown some of them, such as inflammation and bleeding. Yet the cause of most preterm births remained elusive.

The team ran a multidimensional proteomic analysis of amniotic fluid. They charted many proteins at once in cases of idiopathic preterm birth, where no cause is known. Protein patterns may sort hidden causes into groups that can be treated. A clearer split of causes is a step toward stopping early birth.
plos-pone-0002149:
Arun Krishnan, Alessandro Giuliani, Joseph Zbilut, and co-authors looked at a protein as a network, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Their subject was ubiquitin, a small protein found in all complex cells, and the question was how it unfolds. Knowing how proteins are built inside may one day explain how they fold into shape.

Earlier studies by the group treated protein structure as a web of linked parts. Here they ran unfolding simulations and read them with network-based tools. The view shows which links hold the structure together longest. Work of this kind may help predict where a protein will give way under stress.
plos-pone-0002249:
Elife Bagci, Yoram Vodovotz, and Timothy Billiar modeled the double-edged effect of nitric oxide on cell death, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Nitric oxide is a small signaling molecule made throughout the body. It plainly matters in apoptosis, the orderly self-destruction of cells, yet it can both promote and block that death. The reason for the split was elusive.

The authors propose a mathematical model that simulates nitric oxide's competing effects. In the model, dose and timing decide whether the molecule pushes a cell toward death or shields it. A working model helps predict outcomes in inflammation and cancer, where nitric oxide is always in play.
plos-pone-0002349:
Allen Braun, Joe McArdle, Jennifer Jones, and co-authors recorded brain responses in people who cannot carry a tune, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Tune deafness is a central hearing disorder: sufferers cannot discriminate pitch, reproduce melodies, or notice wrong notes, despite normal hearing at the ear. Its cause was unknown.

The team used components of the auditory event-related potential, waves of brain activity after a sound, to see how melodic errors are processed. They found signs that such errors are handled outside conscious awareness. The result places the fault in the brain's early, automatic stages of pitch processing rather than in attention or memory.
plos-pone-0002449:
Poncela and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Julia Poncela, Jesús Gómez-Gardeñes, Luis M. Floría, among others. Its subject is complex Cooperative Networks from Evolutionary Preferential Attachment. How form and function interact during network formation bears on the origin of complex networks, yet it stays largely unstudied.

Past work added dynamics by rewiring a network that already exists, while this team studies network formation itself. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002549:
Krithika and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names S. Krithika, Suvendu Maji, T. S. Vasulu, among others. Its subject is a Microsatellite Guided Insight into the Genetic Status of Adi, an Isolated Hunting-Gathering Tribe of Northeast India. Tibeto-Burman populations of India provide an insight into the peopling of India and aid in understanding their genetic relationship with populations of East.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002649:
In 2008, Alberto Valbuena and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was the C/H3 domain of p300 is required to protect VRK1 and VRK2 from their downregulation induced by p53. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Alberto Valbuena, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. The vaccinia-related kinase 1 (VRK1) protein, an activator of p53, can be proteolytically downregulated by an indirect mechanism, which requires p53-dependent transcription. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002749:
In 2008, Kristen L. Curran and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about circadian genes are expressed during early development in xenopus laevis. The catalog record names Kristen L. Curran first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Circadian oscillators are endogenous time-keeping mechanisms that drive twenty four hour rhythmic changes in gene expression, metabolism, hormone levels, and physical activity. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002849:
In 2008, Yueming Chang and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was messenger RNA oxidation occurs early in disease pathogenesis and promotes motor neuron degeneration in ALS. Authorship is credited in the record to Yueming Chang and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Accumulating evidence indicates that RNA oxidation is involved in a wide variety of neurological diseases and may be associated with neuronal deterioration during the. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002949:
